solutions.check: 32 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 31 answers the paper printed

clue.text: A habit-forming thing for clergymen ?

parts.note: a habit here is a monk's or nun's garment, so the material it is made from forms habits; it is also the collective word for the clergy

explanation.definitionFit: Clergy as a body are called 'the cloth', and fabric is what a religious habit is made from.

clue.text: Old Queen Cole wrong to knock up painter

indicators.note: wrong means set amiss, so the letters of Cole are put in a different order
in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to tap is to knock lightly
RA, Royal Academician, is a painter

explanation.surface: Old King Cole wrongly wakes a painter by knocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' turns COLE into CLEO; 'up' turns TAP into PAT; RA follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra was the last queen of ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Last in some games

indicators.note: in signals the letters lie inside the words some games

explanation.surface: The final round in certain contests.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, so it stands for the end.

clue.text: Fevered — with rash ?

definitions.meaning: having a high temperature in the head, read literally

explanation.definitionFit: Literally a burning head from fever, and idiomatically impetuous and quick-tempered.

clue.text: Rare outfit, smart and striking

indicators.note: to outfit is to fit out afresh, so the letters of the word rare are refitted into a new order

parts.note: to smart is to sting with pain

explanation.surface: An unusual set of clothes, both smart and eye-catching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outfit' looks like a noun for clothes but signals the anagram: RARE becomes ARRE, then STING follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something striking catches the eye and holds the attention, as an arresting sight does.

clue.text: A sorrowful expression?.

parts.note: an expression may be a face, but here it is words saying you are sorry

explanation.definitionFit: Saying sorry for a wrong is making amends in words.

clue.text: Frenchman's an odd sort, and a dramatist

indicators.note: odd means peculiar, so the letters of sort and and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is a strange character, and a playwright too.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmond Rostand wrote Cyrano de Bergerac; 'Frenchman's' helps point to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmond Rostand was the French playwright who wrote Cyrano de Bergerac.

clue.text: Vulgar words of abuse ?

definitions.meaning: to hurl insults at someone, as a verb

explanation.definitionFit: Informal speech outside standard usage, and, as a verb, to rail at with insults.

clue.text: Parson is fashionable, with classical bias

parts.note: in means in fashion
cum is Latin, the classical tongue, for with
a bent is a leaning or bias

explanation.surface: A vicar is trendy and has a leaning towards the classics.
explanation.walkthrough: CUM is Latin for 'with', hence 'classical'.
explanation.definitionFit: An incumbent is the clergyman holding a parish benefice.

clue.text: Proceed to lift for instance a weight

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting raises the letters, so the abbreviation for example is read upwards

parts.note: eg stands for exempli gratia, for instance
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Go on and raise a heavy load.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lift' turns EG upwards into GE; TON follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on or advance is the phrasal verb's meaning.

clue.text: Odd trio seen round about the buildings

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round, enclosing the abbreviation for about
odd means strange or irregular, telling us to jumble the letters of trio and seen

parts.note: C, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: Three strange people are spotted wandering near some buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' scrambles TRIO and SEEN to give ERETIONS, which goes 'round' C (circa, about) to make ERECTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Erections are things that have been put up, in the sense of structures or edifices.

clue.text: Like a humble home, of course

parts.note: as means like, in a comparison
a cot is an old word for a cottage or small humble dwelling

explanation.surface: Something resembling a modest cottage, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally' but the definition is a racecourse: ASCOT, in Berkshire, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a famous English racecourse, scene of the Royal Ascot meeting.

clue.text: Smoother piano passage

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
a lane is a narrow way or passage

explanation.surface: A gentler stretch of music for the pianist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piano passage' looks like music; P (piano, softly) and LANE (a passage) make a carpenter's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter's plane is the tool that smooths wood, so it is a smoother.

clue.text: Was Miss Gwyn supplied by such a Protestant?

definitions.text: Was Miss Gwyn supplied by such a Protestant?

parts.words: Was Miss Gwyn supplied by such a Protestant?
parts.note: Nell Gwyn sold citrus fruit at Drury Lane, so a seller of that fruit might have supplied her; the same compound names a member of the Ulster loyalist Protestant order

explanation.walkthrough: Nell Gwyn, Charles II's mistress, began as a seller of oranges at a London theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: An Orangeman belongs to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternal society in Northern Ireland named after William of Orange.

clue.text: Producer of a graceful child ?

parts.note: the nursery rhyme says a child born on a certain weekday is full of grace, so that day produces graceful children

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' continues 'Tuesday's child is full of grace'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional nursery rhyme, a child born on the third weekday is full of grace.

clue.text: To explain intricate clue I need time

indicators.note: intricate means tangled, so the letters of clue and I are rearranged

parts.note: a date is a point in time

explanation.surface: A solver needs time to unpick a tricky crossword hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intricate' turns CLUE and I into ELUCI, then DATE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To make clear, to throw light on: from Latin lux, light.

clue.text: Noble record of strange breed and race

indicators.note: strange means odd or unusual, telling us to rearrange the letters of breed

parts.note: TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: An account of an odd pedigree and lineage among the nobility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' turns BREED into DEBRE, then TT (Tourist Trophy) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Debrett's is the long-established guide listing the British peerage and aristocracy.

clue.text: To this an accolade we hear for the ignorant

indicators.note: we hear signals a word sounding like another

parts.note: an accolade is the touch of a sword conferring knighthood, so it leads one to be dubbed a knight

explanation.surface: Praise is heard to be given to the uneducated.
explanation.walkthrough: The accolade is the dubbing that knights someone; 'be knighted' sounds like the answer, with its silent K.
explanation.definitionFit: Benighted means in intellectual or moral darkness, unenlightened.

clue.text: Hill meets teacher he teased

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
a mentor is a trusted teacher or guide

explanation.surface: A man named Hill meets the teacher he used to mock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he teased' defines someone who torments.
explanation.definitionFit: A tormentor is one who torments, harassing and taunting.

clue.text: Divided into parts as foreign articles

parts.note: un is a French indefinite article
der is a German definite article

explanation.surface: Split up in the way that overseas items are.
explanation.walkthrough: AS is taken as written; 'foreign articles' supplies two: French UN and German DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn apart into separate pieces, as in the wedding vow's 'let no man put asunder'.

clue.text: I greet a reformer in a Surrey town

indicators.note: a reformer remakes things, so the letters of I greet a are formed anew

explanation.surface: Someone welcomes a political reformer in a home-counties town.
explanation.walkthrough: REIGATE is a market town in Surrey, south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Reigate is a market town in the English county of Surrey, south of London.

clue.text: Senior pupil takes car outside in reverse

indicators.note: the car's letters go outside, wrapping round the reversed word

parts.note: a motor is a car

indicators.note: in reverse means the little word in is read backwards

explanation.surface: A head boy drives a car backwards out of the school gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in reverse' turns IN into NI, which MOTOR goes 'outside': MO-NI-TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools a monitor is a pupil given duties of supervising others.

clue.text: Fighter given to wild talk Is leaving the country

parts.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter plane
a rant is wild, ranting talk

explanation.surface: A pilot prone to raving is emigrating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' and 'given to' join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A migrant moves from place to place, here one heading abroad.

clue.text: Sounding surprised, seeing game-fish

parts.note: whist is a card game
a ling is a long food fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Someone gasps at the sight of a sporting fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game-fish' looks like one thing (a fish caught for sport) but splits into a card game and a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone surprised may let out a low whistle, so whistling is making that astonished sound.

clue.text: Archaic fellow, our southern islander ?

definitions.meaning: an old word for a person or creature
the Isle of ... lies off the south coast of England

explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a person, and the island off England's south coast.

clue.text: Endeavour to get good man for appointment

parts.note: to try is to endeavour
ST, saint, is a good man

explanation.surface: Try to secure a decent chap for the job.
explanation.walkthrough: ST (saint) is the crossword's good man.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is an arranged meeting, typically a lovers' rendezvous.

clue.text: Appearance of a French duke?

definitions.meaning: the Duc de ... headed a powerful noble family in sixteenth-century France

explanation.definitionFit: A guise is an outward look, and Guise was a ducal title borne by French nobles.

clue.text: Single French boy meeting girl

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
René is a French boy's name

explanation.surface: An unmarried French lad meets a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is a girl's name.

clue.text: Runs out of beef?

parts.note: reads as a shortage of meat, but means the juice that runs out of roasting meat

explanation.definitionFit: Gravy is made from the juices that drip from a joint as it roasts.

clue.text: 18 chaps to drop round to this room

parts.note: the answer to clue 18, divided into parts, here in its sense of separately
chaps are men

indicators.note: the word to drops a letter, losing the round one

parts.note: O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Some men are invited to call in at this room.
explanation.walkthrough: The 18 answer gives APART; MEN follows; 'to drop round' means TO loses O (round), leaving T.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment is a room or set of rooms forming a dwelling.

clue.text: Well, you won't need this!

parts.note: reads as a casual remark, but if you are well you need no medical care

explanation.definitionFit: Medical care is what the sick receive, and the healthy go without it.

clue.text: Gloomy view of expensive outside-right

indicators.note: outside-right is read as the costly word going outside the letter for right

parts.note: dear means costly

explanation.surface: A bleak opinion about a pricey winger in football.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside-right' is an old football position; split, DEAR goes 'outside' R.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic word for dreary, meaning dismal and cheerless.
